newsitem.title: GERMANY: Compaq aims at higher European market share.
newsitem.headline: Compaq aims at higher European market share.

text.p: BONN, Germany, Feb 28 - Compaq Computer Corp, hoping to rebound after a tough year in Germany, plans to roll out new low-cost personal computers next week aimed at home users, company officials said on Friday.

The Presario 2110 computers would give German consumers complete multimedia systems with sound, video, fax and Internet capabilities for 2,200 marks -- a price Compaq did not offer last year when its home PC market share in Germany fell by more than half.
The price is almost exactly the same as Compaq's U.S. price for the same model, but value-added taxes would boost it higher.

"We expect to make significant market share gains," Compaq vice president for consumer products Toon Bouten told Reuters. Last year Compaq had too few offerings in the consumer segment, and its lowest-priced model was 3,500 marks. But the Presario will help correct that this year, he said.
Still, analysts were not convinced the new machines would strengthen Compaq against established German suppliers Vobis Microcomputer AG and Siemens Nixdorf Informationssysteme AG

"I would not assume it will be easy for Compaq to regain market share," said James Bates at market researcher Context in London. "Compaq will get to a level of consumer it wasn't targeting before, but there are plenty of other PCs on the market at this price."
Compaq would also have to contend with Germany's sluggish economy, where consumer spending remains wilted, he said.

The company would release the Presario 2110 computers -- which use a processor from Cyrix Corp instead of Intel Corp -- first in Germany, France, Britain, Austria and the Netherlands. They should arrive in other countries over the next six months.

The Presario 2110 models use Cyrix's MediaGX chip, a 133MHz chip compatible with the Pentium processors most PCs use. They also include 24 megabytes of memory, a modem, a two-gigabyte hard drive and a CD-ROM drive.

Bates said he did not expect home buyers to shy away from the Compaq PCs because they don't have an Intel microchip. "At these prices, people are more worried about what they can do with the computer than what processor it has," he said.

Last year, when Compaq only offered a few high-priced models for home buyers, its share in the segment in Germany fell to 3.5 percent from 7.5 percent in 1995, according to market researcher Dataquest.
Compaq ranked eleventh in home PC sales last year, down from number three the year before. Vobis was number one with 19.9 percent of the German home market.
In the total German market last year, Compaq ranked third with a 7.8 percent share. SNI held 12.1 percent and Vobis 12 percent, Dataquest said.
